For some the achievement was relevant to that person, and for others it was not. People said they would show less pride when the achievement was relevant to the person watching.

p117831118.post: Some people wrote a letter to their future self and others did not. Then they made choices that could be delinquent. People who wrote to their future self were less inclined to make delinquent choices.

p154f8890d.post: Men crossing a scary suspension bridge or a non-scary bridge were approached by an attractive woman interviewer. She asked them to fill out a questionnaire that included writing stories about pictures. The men on the scary bridge wrote stories with more sexual content and were more likely to try to contact her afterward.

p19789ad5a.post: People chose from a set of options that were shown either one at a time or all at once. Then they rated how satisfied they were with their choice and how committed they felt to it. People shown the options one at a time were less satisfied and less committed.

p1cc37feb5.post: People watched a video that included a salient person. Later, some described that person's face and others did not. Then everyone tried to recognize the face. People who had described the face did worse at recognizing it.

p24ec0c969.post: Some people ate a sweet food, some a food that was not sweet, and some no food. Then they rated how agreeable they were. People who had eaten the sweet food rated themselves as more agreeable and helped more.

p272ce9c73.post: People watched a rapid stream of images and tried to spot a target that came right after an irrelevant picture. They did this when hungry and when full. Pictures of food made hungry people worse at spotting the target.

p27485cdac.post: People read scenarios in their native language or in a foreign language. In each, they imagined doing something under a superstitious circumstance, such as a broken mirror or a four-leaf clover, and rated how they would feel. A foreign language led to less negative feelings about bad-luck scenarios and less positive feelings about good-luck scenarios.

p296e0c072.post: People chose between gambles described in terms of gains or in terms of losses. Some choices had to be made under time pressure and others not. The way a gamble was described shifted people's choices more when they had to decide fast.

p2d8e62ae6.post: People decided whether a word was a brand name. Brand names were shown in their usual case, such as adidas and IKEA, or in the other case, such as ADIDAS and ikea. People identified brand names faster in their usual case.

p312808aa8.post: High school students either played a game in which they made a misleading news article about a politicized issue, or did not. Then they rated how reliable and persuasive fake news articles were. Students who had played the game rated fake news articles as less reliable and less persuasive.

p32f15d1d7.post: People from age 7 to adulthood saw a set of shelves with objects and moved objects as a director instructed. The director could see only some of the objects, so people had to move only the ones the director could see. Teenagers aged 14 to 17 made more errors than adults.

p37ebefb1d.post: People read about a person's behaviors and judged how much each behavior reflected the person's true self. People judged morally good behaviors as reflecting the true self more than morally bad ones.

p3a105046d.post: Athletes with no track experience did sprint starts, once before and once after a first task. For some, the first task was meant to use up self-control, and for others it was not. Only those whose self-control had been used up became more likely to start before the signal.

p3bd6c6916.post: Japanese people rated how much they liked different Japanese letters. They liked the letters included in their own name more than the other letters.

p3f2802938.post: Infants were held and gently bounced to music while facing an experimenter, who bounced either in sync or out of sync with the infant. Then the experimenter 'accidentally' dropped objects, and researchers watched whether the infants handed them back. Infants bounced in sync with the experimenter were more likely to help.

p4274e34b3.post: People did a task of spotting changes in a display while holding both hands either near the display or away from it. People were more accurate at detecting changes, and held more items in short-term memory, when their hands were near the display.

p44a8dad93.post: Children of different ages saw two rows of objects, one longer and one with more objects, and said which row had more. Children of about two and a half to three picked the row with more objects. Children aged about three to four and a half picked the longer row even though it had fewer. Older children again picked correctly.

p46c3ede86.post: People read about actions that happened at a nearby place or a distant one, and chose whether to identify each action by what it was for or by how it was done. People more often identified actions by what they were for when the place was distant.

p4b35c8a2b.post: Parish councils in England were sent requests for information, some as formal Freedom of Information requests and others as simple informal asks. The formal requests were more effective at getting the information than the informal asks.

p4bebdf2ed.post: People learned verbal material and were tested after a period of sleep or a period awake. Some were also exposed to interference before the test. Recall was better after sleep than after being awake, and the gap was even bigger when interference was added.

p4faf74fe4.post: People read about a favor done for them, either for kind reasons or for ulterior motives. Then they rated how grateful and how indebted they felt. People felt more grateful when the helper had kind intentions, but felt equally indebted either way.

p506e5e803.post: Students were given hypnotic suggestions to respond to. For some the suggestions went from easy to difficult, and for others from difficult to easy. The two groups' total scores did not differ.

p50d149c05.post: People were randomly given oxytocin or a placebo and were asked to trust someone with confidential information. People who got oxytocin were more trusting that their privacy would not be violated.

p5a0cea8bb.post: Japanese participants imagined a scenario in which they had either caused harm to someone or not. Then they decided how to share resources between themselves and the other person. People who had caused harm gave more of their resources to the other person at their own expense.

p62c72748d.post: People rated how intense the emotion was in instrumental music, or in the same music with lyrics. Lyrics made happy and calm music less emotional, but made sad and angry music more emotional.

p65b16319b.post: People saw some fake-news headlines one time or four times, and other headlines not at all. Later they rated how unethical it would be to publish and share each headline. People rated the headlines they had seen before as less unethical to share, even when the headlines were clearly labeled as false.

p6e3da285a.post: People decided as fast as they could whether strings of letters were real words. Some words were more iconic, meaning their sound resembles their meaning. People responded faster and more accurately to the more iconic words.

p6f50545a4.post: Undergraduates read a persuasive message that argued against what they already believed. Some read strong arguments and some weak ones, and the message came from a source that was either an expert or not. For some students the issue mattered a lot to them personally, and for others it hardly did. When the issue mattered to them, students were swayed mostly by how strong the arguments were, and when it did not, they were swayed mostly by how expert the source seemed.

p70218946d.post: University students were randomly assigned to study groups. Students became more conscientious when assigned to conscientious peers, more open-minded when assigned to open-minded peers, and more competitive when assigned to competitive peers.

p740db5049.post: Children and adults learned about two made-up groups, Hibbles and Glerks, that typically ate different kinds of berries. They then judged individuals who ate the berries typical of their own group or of the other group. Children judged the individuals who ate the other group's berries negatively, less so as they got older.

p74f4c64ce.post: People traded in experimental markets where they could know about upcoming dividends. In some markets everyone knew, in some no one knew, and in some only some traders knew. Bubbles were smaller in the markets where only some traders knew more than the others.

p777411842.post: People read explanations for why a person behaved a certain way. Some explanations appealed to a named tendency or condition, and others gave the same explanation without the name. People found the explanations with the name more satisfying.

p7a6dbf0f8.post: People who were high or low in social anxiety gave an impromptu speech. Researchers measured how anxious they felt and acted, how aroused they thought their bodies were, and how aroused their bodies actually were. High-anxiety people felt and acted more anxious and thought they were more aroused, but their actual physiological activation did not differ.

p7b88dedbf.post: Infants aged 6 and 12 months saw novel actions demonstrated. Some then took a nap of at least 30 minutes and others did not. Later they were tested on whether they remembered the actions. Only infants who had napped remembered the actions.

p7cb125292.post: Some people were given reminders that atheists are common, and others were not. Then they rated how much they distrust atheists. People reminded of how common atheists are distrusted them less.

p7cd1acb8d.post: Working-class and middle-class Americans decided which products to buy after learning what other people had chosen. Working-class Americans were more influenced by others' choices than middle-class Americans.

p7cf2e81a9.post: Preschoolers heard a made-up verb in a sentence while watching events, such as 'the girl is fezzing' or 'the tall girl is fezzing'. Then they pointed to the event they thought the verb meant. Children picked the right event for 'the girl is fezzing' but not for 'the tall girl is fezzing'.

p84159028b.post: Undergraduates filled in two questionnaires: one on how they treat themselves when things go wrong, and one on their health habits. Researchers looked at which parts of self-compassion went with a healthier lifestyle. Students who were kind to themselves, saw their struggles as part of being human, and were mindful lived healthier lives.

p846fd2bd7.post: People sang two popular songs from memory, and their pitch was compared with the pitch of the original recordings. Many people sang at least one song at the right pitch.

p887f3f577.post: Women saw photographs of men who were more or less attractive, each with a description of how he behaved in different situations, altruistically or not. They rated how desirable each man was. Women preferred the altruistic men, especially for long-term relationships.

p8d09c3b4a.post: People solved math problems that have an intuitively tempting wrong answer, and also reported how strongly they believe in God. People who gave more of the tempting intuitive answers reported stronger belief in God.

p9029f7700.post: People's pupils were measured while they read single words that conveyed brightness, such as day, darkness, such as night, or neither, such as house. Pupils were largest for the dark words, in between for neutral words, and smallest for the bright words.

p9184a27b1.post: People held either expansive, open poses or contracted, closed poses. Then they prepared and gave a speech to two evaluators in a mock job interview. People who had held the expansive poses performed better and were more likely to be chosen for hire.

p95498aeb7.post: People told the truth about a route they had taken, and also lied about it, describing it either in normal order or in reverse order. Other people then read the transcripts and judged which accounts were lies. Observers detected lies better when the route was described in reverse order.

p97bcb718e.post: People viewed a few organic foods, comfort foods, or control foods. Then they were asked to volunteer time to help a needy stranger. People who had seen organic foods volunteered less time.

p9843f1b69.post: Some people were reminded of their own death and others were not. Then they answered questions about a group they belonged to. People reminded of death identified more strongly with their group and showed more bias in favor of it.

p9ba3b95b4.post: Infants raised with one language or two learned to look at one side of a screen ahead of time because a cue predicted a reward there. Then the cue began to predict the reward on the opposite side. Only the bilingual infants managed to switch their looks to the new side.

p9d528fc73.post: Some people first had the chance to disagree with blatantly sexist statements, and others did not. Later they chose whether to favor a man or a woman for a stereotypically male job. People who had first disagreed with the sexist statements were more willing to favor the man.

p9f41d416e.post: People heard either a word such as 'cat' or a sound such as a cat meowing, and then saw a picture and said whether it matched. People verified the picture faster and more accurately after the word than after the sound.

pa0a292be2.post: University students solved logic problems presented in text, in formulas, or in combinations such as text with formulas or text with graphics. Students given a combination of representations outperformed students given just one.

pa5bd01a96.post: Children aged 6 to 11 were told about the carrots other children had eaten: a large amount, none, or no information. Then they got carrots to eat. Children who thought other children had eaten a large amount of carrots ate more carrots than all the others.

pa5fd08df3.post: People had a chance to cheat by overreporting how well they did on a task. Then they did tasks that measure creativity. People who cheated were more creative afterward than people who did not.

pa69956311.post: Adults looked at photographs of trees shown in patterns based on the seasons, or in random order, and rated how meaningful their lives felt. People who saw the patterned photographs reported more meaning in life.

pab759937a.post: People wrote statements about an event, some as mock criminals who were lying and some as innocent people telling the truth. Half of each group were told beforehand that their statements would be checked for details that could be verified. Being told made truth tellers, but not liars, give more details that could be checked.

pb29f01275.post: In New Haven, registered voters were randomly assigned to receive a get-out-the-vote message just before an election, from a canvasser in person, by mail, or by telephone. Then researchers checked who voted. Voter turnout rose substantially with canvassing, slightly with mail, and not at all with phone calls.

pb66f6f4bc.post: Some people were first asked how much they would donate to help one needy person, and then how much to donate to help a whole group of needy people. Others were asked only about the group. People who were asked about one person first gave more to the group.

pb6a03b3f7.post: People thought about their own death or about dental pain. Then they chose between $50 now and increasingly attractive rewards in three months. People who had thought about death accepted a smaller later reward in place of the $50 than people who had thought about dental pain.

pb89f51c24.post: Native English speakers heard odd sentences, like 'the mother gave the candle the daughter', and said what they thought was meant. Some were spoken with a foreign accent and others with a native accent. People were more likely to take the odd sentence as the sensible one when the speaker had a foreign accent.

pb9ba564a1.post: Students first did a brief task that made them anxious. Then some colored a mandala, some colored a plaid pattern, and some colored on a blank piece of paper. Anxiety went down about equally for the mandala and plaid colorers, and more than for the blank-paper colorers.

pbaabe24f1.post: People saw faces of other people described as students at their own university or at a different one. Later they tried to recognize the faces. People recognized faces of their own university's students better.

pbba258e36.post: People had a chance to claim money they were not entitled to. Some were told 'Please don't be a cheater' and others 'Please don't cheat'. People told 'Please don't cheat' claimed more money than people told 'Please don't be a cheater'.

pbba789cda.post: Toddlers learned a new word for an object from a speaker who had been either accurate or inaccurate before. Then they were tested on what the word meant. Toddlers responded less systematically when the speaker had been inaccurate.

pbecc04662.post: Adults did a creativity test in which they came up with uses for everyday objects, once while sitting and once while walking on a treadmill. Most people scored higher on creativity while walking than while sitting.

pc0ade8d90.post: Silver and bronze medalists at the 1992 Summer Olympics were observed right after their events and on the medal stand, and their emotional reactions were analyzed. Bronze medalists tended to be happier than silver medalists.

pc19669eb8.post: People watched campaign advertisements that were the same in every way except for their tone, negative or not. Then they said how likely they were to vote. People who saw the negative ads reported lower intentions to vote.

pc28ea6705.post: Women were led to value happiness, or were given no such prompt. Then some did something designed to make them feel happy and others something to make them feel sad, and they reported how they felt. Women led to value happiness reacted less positively to the happy activity, but not to the sad one.

pc2ee1d4bd.post: People learned to sort 'aliens' into ones to approach and ones to avoid. After each answer they got feedback, and then a nonsense label was either shown or not. People who saw the labels learned the categories better, even though the labels added no new information.

pc810308cc.post: People saw slides of a car hitting a pedestrian. Afterward some got information consistent with what they saw, some got misleading information, and some got irrelevant information. Then they took a recognition test. People who got misleading information were less accurate.

pcacbb3d19.post: People read about a local recycling program and the officials running it. Some saw more female first names among the officials, and others saw fewer. Then they rated how willing they were to recycle and compost. Women were more willing to cooperate when more of the officials had female names.

pccd080bde.post: People read about someone whose action brought a personal benefit and also helped charity, or about a similar action that brought only the personal benefit. Then they evaluated the behavior. People judged the action that also helped charity as worse.

pccf366b6b.post: People watched a distressing film. Then some thought about it on purpose, some did a demanding task knowing the film would matter later, and some did it believing the study was over. Those who did the task knowing the film would matter had fewer unwanted memories of the film than the others.

pcd3735d69.post: People learned computer skills in one of two ways. One group was guided to avoid errors. The other group was given problems too hard to solve without making errors. The group that practiced with errors scored higher on tests that were not timed.

pd27671c51.post: People first did a task meant to use up their self-control, or a control task. Then they worked on matchstick arithmetic puzzles, which are solved by suddenly seeing the problem in a new way. People whose self-control had been used up solved more of them correctly.

pd55f8c3e4.post: Beginning algebra students solved simple problems presented either as story problems or as equations that mean the same thing. Students were more successful at solving the story problems than the equations.

pd8ee825f2.post: Children aged 6 and 10 listened to stories in which a character hides how they feel. They were asked how the character would look and how the character would really feel. Both age groups could tell the difference quite accurately.

pd91b977ab.post: People answered 22 standard questions that test cognitive biases, such as overconfidence and anchoring. Some were first told to notice three new things, which was meant to make them mindful. Mindful people were less likely to show the bias on most of the questions.

pda46001d8.post: People read a sentence that implied an object's color, then saw a picture of the object in a color that either matched or mismatched, and said whether the object had been mentioned. They responded faster when the colors mismatched than when they matched.

pdc848472b.post: People were assigned to a high-power role or a low-power role. Then they chose between smaller immediate rewards and larger future rewards. People in high-power roles were less likely to prefer the smaller immediate reward.

pe0d7b180f.post: Some people were led to think about having power and others were not. Then they played a golf putting game. People who had been led to think about power putted better.

pe2c85a598.post: Smokers saw cigarette package warnings with pictures that were more or less graphic, or with no picture. Then they reported how much they intended to quit smoking. More graphic pictures strengthened smokers' intentions to quit.

pe48fb5dbd.post: Asian American participants were prompted to think about their American self, their Asian self, or things in nature. Then they recalled important events from their lives. Those prompted to think about their American self recalled more self-focused and less socially oriented memories than those prompted to think about their Asian self.

pe50892472.post: In the Netherlands, Muslims and non-Muslims rated how much they believed conspiracy theories, some about Muslims or Jewish people and some unrelated, such as that the moon landings were fake. Muslims believed both kinds more strongly than non-Muslims did.

pe57b6b57c.post: People first did a task that used up their self-control, or a control task. Then they reported how well they had done on another task, with money at stake. People whose self-control had been used up overstated their performance more.

pe77949923.post: Adults learned about the structure and function of the human heart from paper materials. Some were told to gesture, such as pointing and tracing, as they learned, and others were not. Then they took a knowledge test. People instructed to gesture performed better.

pe83fa6eb6.post: People chose two candy bars. For some, the choice was framed as picking two single candy bars, and for others as picking one bundle of two. People picked more variety when they chose single candy bars than when they chose a bundle.

pec602469b.post: People read about a deceased person and several candidates who might be that person's reincarnation, each matching the deceased in one feature. They chose the candidate most likely to be the reincarnation. Candidates sharing a physical mark, such as a mole, or a specific autobiographical memory were chosen more often than candidates sharing other features.

pee2d20adb.post: People about to sing karaoke, give a speech, or do math either tried to calm down or told themselves they were excited, for example by saying 'I am excited' out loud. People who told themselves they were excited felt more excited and performed better than people who tried to calm down.

pef1254bd7.post: People recalled a series of related events from their lives, either in reverse order ending with a target event, or in chronological order starting with it. Then they rated how far away the target event felt. The event felt closer when people recalled the series backward.

pef860b2f5.post: People described an intention in an interview, some telling the truth about what they planned to do and some lying about it. Researchers counted how many details about places and times each person gave. People telling the truth gave more spatial and temporal details.

pf001587df.post: People saw two digits and then a symbol, and said as fast as they could whether the symbol was a number. Before it, a word flashed too briefly to see: either 'add' or a control word. When the symbol was the sum of the two digits and the hidden word was 'add', people identified it faster.

pf65bd4aca.post: People turned a crank either clockwise or counterclockwise. Then they chose between familiar things and new ones. People who turned the crank counterclockwise preferred the familiar, while people who turned it clockwise preferred the new.

pf7c8f385c.post: People negotiated on a computer and were told whether their opponent was angry, happy, or neither. People gave in more to an angry opponent than to a happy one.

pf85070837.post: People chose between a basic option and a premium option, such as direct flights. For some, the premium price was shown as the extra cost, 'for $20 more'. For others it was shown as the total, 'for $60 total'. More people chose the premium option when its price was shown as the extra cost.

pfbaf6e6f7.post: People reported on their current and past romantic relationships, saying who confessed love first and how they felt when a partner said 'I love you'. People thought women confess love first and feel happier when they hear it, but in real relationships men confessed first and felt happier hearing it.

pfcb38528a.post: American and Chinese college students answered a survey about dating attitudes and behaviors. American students had more liberal views, started dating younger, dated more often, and were more likely to have sex with their dates than Chinese students.

pfd1be9e46.post: People studied prose passages. Then some repeatedly restudied the material and others repeatedly took tests on it. One week later everyone took a final test with new questions that required drawing inferences. People who had repeatedly taken tests did better than people who had repeatedly restudied.
